pair.title: Where the sea horizon sits
pair.mini: Same eye height, two worlds. On a plane the sea runs out to meet eye level: there is no angle to measure. On a globe the horizon lies an angle δ below eye level, the dip, and navigators correct for it every day.
pair.text: Where the sea horizon sits relative to eye level, for the same eye height in both panels. On a plane the sea runs out to meet the eye-level line and there is no angle between them to measure, at any height. On a globe the horizon is the point where a line from the eye touches the sea, and it lies an angle δ below eye level: the dip. It grows with the square root of the eye height. Curvature is exaggerated in the drawing.
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a sea horizon measured at eye level, with zero dip, from any height.
flatten.title: Flatten the Earth, and the horizon climbs back to eye level
flatten.mini: From the Sommet de Viériou, 1,395 m up, the sea horizon sits 1.20° below eye level on the globe. Flatten the Earth and it climbs; on a plane it never leaves eye level.
flatten.text: The same eye, 1,395 m up on the Sommet de Viériou above the Mediterranean, while the curvature goes from the real Earth to a plane and back. On the globe the sea horizon sits 1.20° below eye level, 1.12° with standard refraction (k = 0.13) [1]. As the surface flattens the horizon climbs, and on a plane it never leaves eye level. In between, the surface is a larger sphere, never a stretched drawing; the side view's exaggeration is printed on it, and the angles come from the geometry, not from the drawing.
flatten.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the sea horizon measured at eye level from a mountain top.
globe.title: The dip on the globe
globe.mini: On a globe, raise your eye and the horizon moves away, as √h, while the line of sight to it tips further below horizontal. Eye height, dip and horizon distance are printed on the image.
globe.text: On a globe the surface keeps its shape; only the observer moves. Raise the eye and the point where the line of sight touches the sea slides outward, as the square root of the height, while the line of sight tips further below horizontal. The dip is about √(2h/R) in radians, and the horizon lies at about √(2Rh) [1]. Everything beyond the horizon is geometrically hidden. The eye height, the dip and the horizon distance shown are printed on the image; the curvature is exaggerated by the factor printed there.
globe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a dip that does not grow with the square root of the eye height.
plane.title: No dip on a plane
plane.mini: On a flat plane the observer rises, but no horizon point ever forms: the surface runs straight to the edge of view, and the only horizon is eye level itself, reached at infinity. The dip is zero at every height.
plane.text: The same frame and the same scales as a globe, but flat. The observer rises and nothing else changes: no tangent point ever forms, the surface runs straight to the edge of the frame, and the only horizon is the eye-level line itself, reached at infinity. The dip is zero at every height. At the distance where a globe's horizon would sit, the plane still shows open ground a small angle below eye level, and it carries on. The eye height shown is printed on the image.
plane.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a horizon measured at eye level, at every height.
both.title: The horizon dips on a globe, never on a plane
both.mini: The same eye height. On the globe, the sea horizon lies a measurable angle below eye level. On the plane, it stays at eye level. Navigators subtract that dip from every sextant sight.
both.text: The same observer at the same height, on a globe and on a plane. On the globe the line of sight to the sea horizon touches the surface at a tangent point and leaves eye level by the dip, about √(2h/R) [1]. On the plane no tangent point forms: the surface runs to infinity and the only horizon is eye level, so the dip is zero at every height. The dip is not a theoretical nicety: it is tabulated in navigation manuals, and every sextant altitude taken from a ship's deck is corrected for it [2]. The eye height, the dip and the horizon distance are printed on the images.
both.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: sextant sights that come out right without the dip correction.
tangent.title: The dip, from one tangent line
tangent.mini: An eye at height h above a sphere of radius R. The line of sight that grazes the surface leaves eye level by the dip δ and touches the surface at the horizon: cos δ = R/(R + h).
tangent.text: An eye at height h above a sphere of radius R. The line of sight that just grazes the surface is tangent to it, so it is perpendicular to the radius at the horizon. That right triangle, with sides R and R + h, gives everything: cos δ = R/(R + h) for the dip, and a horizon at a straight-line distance of about √(2Rh). For small heights, δ ≈ √(2h/R) in radians [1]. Refraction bends the sightline and replaces R by R/(1 − k), which reduces the dip by several percent but never cancels it. The drawing is schematic.
tangent.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dip angles that do not follow cos δ = R/(R + h) as the eye rises.
chord.title: The same dip on a plane: a contradiction
chord.mini: Grant the flat model the measured dip. On a plane, that sightline hits the ground at a finite distance, h/tan δ, and the ground simply carries on beyond it. There is no edge there.
chord.text: Suppose the flat model accepts the dip, since it is measured. On a plane, a line of sight tipped down by δ strikes the ground at a distance h/tan δ, and the ground simply carries on beyond that point. Nothing marks it, and it is not where the horizon is observed to be. The flat model then has three statements it cannot reconcile: the dip is real, the horizon is ranged at a certain distance, and a plane has no edge at either. The drawing is schematic.
chord.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a visible edge of the ground at the distance h/tan δ.
tri.title: Solve the triangle: a factor of exactly 2
tri.mini: Take the measured dip and do flat trigonometry: the ground contact lands at half the distance where the horizon is actually ranged. The factor is 2 at every height, the signature of a tangent to a circle.
tri.text: Grant the flat model the measured dip δ. Flat trigonometry puts the point where that sightline meets the ground at h/tan δ. The horizon actually ranged, by radar, known landmarks or ships disappearing, sits twice as far. Since δ ≈ √(2h/R), h/tan δ ≈ √(Rh/2), exactly half of √(2Rh), whatever the height. On the plane the surface ends at neither distance; on a globe both numbers describe the same tangent point. The factor of 2 is not a fudge: it is the signature of a tangent line on a circle against a chord to a plane. The numbers for the height shown are printed on the image.
tri.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a ranged horizon at h/tan δ, where flat trigonometry puts it.
env.title: The surface you never drew
env.mini: Seven sightlines to the horizon from real vantage points on one vertical, from a beach to an airliner, each tipped by its own dip. No surface is drawn, yet the lines leave a curved void below them: the Earth.
env.text: Seven real vantage points on one vertical, from a beach to an airliner, each with its line of sight to the sea horizon, tipped below horizontal by its own dip. No ground is drawn at all. Yet the lines leave a wedge below them that none of them enters, and its upper boundary curves: it is the envelope of all the tangent lines, and the only surface they can all be tangent to is a circle of one radius. On a plane every line would be horizontal and they would all coincide.
env.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: sightlines to the horizon that are all horizontal, whatever the height.
radius.title: Measuring the Earth from one dip angle
radius.mini: Measure your height and the dip of the sea horizon and you can solve for the Earth's radius: R ≈ 2h/δ². No satellite, no travel. The test is that it comes out the same from a cliff, a mountain or an aircraft.
radius.text: Turn the dip formula around. From cos δ = R/(R + h), the radius is R = h·cos δ/(1 − cos δ), about 2h/δ² with δ in radians. Measure your height and the dip, and R follows, with no satellites, no travel and no second observer [1]. Al-Bīrūnī did it around 1018 from a hill in the Salt Range. The naive answer comes out about 15% too large, because refraction reduces the dip; the correction is known [1]. A single value would prove little: the test is that the same R comes out from a sea cliff, a mountain and an aircraft window. A variant needs only a stopwatch: watch the sunset lying down, then stand up and time the second sunset [2]. The drawing is schematic.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dips from different heights giving radii that disagree, or none at all.
window.title: Below eye level and still in the sky
window.mini: Between eye level and the sea horizon lies a band of sky that is below you. The Sun, 32′ across, fits in it once the band is one Sun-width tall: from an eye height of about 330 m.
window.text: If the horizon sits δ below eye level, there is a band of sky, δ tall, that is below the level line and above the horizon at the same time. The Sun spans about 32′ [1], so its whole disc is below eye level once its centre is 16′ below, and still wholly clear of the horizon until its centre is 16′ above it. The Sun fits in the band once the dip reaches one Sun-width, from an eye height of about 330 m. From a mountain or an airliner, the whole Sun is seen, against sky, while a bubble level says it is beneath you. On a plane the band has zero height. The drawing is schematic.
window.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun never seen whole below eye level, from any height.
band.title: The band the Sun has to cross
band.mini: The band between eye level and the sea horizon, drawn at true scale for the eye height printed on the image. On a flat plane the two lines coincide and the band has zero height, at every altitude.
band.text: The band of sky between eye level and the sea horizon, at true angular scale, for the eye height and dip printed on the image. Below about 330 m the band is narrower than the Sun, 32′ across [1], so the disc cannot fit inside it; higher up it can, and from an aircraft the band is several Sun-widths tall. Anything in it, the Sun, the Moon or a distant aircraft, is seen whole, against sky, while a level says it is below you. Refraction lifts objects near the horizon and shrinks the dip by about 8% [2]; both work against the effect rather than creating it. On a flat plane the two lines coincide and the band has zero height, at every altitude.
band.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: no measurable band between eye level and the sea horizon, from any height.
caus.title: Bend the Earth under a real view, then show the photograph
caus.mini: The view east from 1,210 m above the Riviera, computed on a plane, then on the measured Earth, then with refraction; then the photograph. Its sea horizon and Mont Agel land where the globe puts them, about 45′ from the plane.
caus.text: The view east from 1,210 m on the plateau de Caussols, drawn from the IGN's 1 m LiDAR and, beyond 45 km, the Copernicus 30 m model [1][2]. On a plane the sea rises towards eye level, and Mont Agel, 77 m lower than the eye (1,133 m in the terrain model, 1,148 m published) and 39 km away [3], sits 7′ below the horizon. Curved to the Earth's measured radius, 6,371 km, the horizon falls 67′ below eye level; refraction (k = 0.13) acts as a larger radius and lifts it back to 62′. Then Xyphophor's photograph, framed with the camera's own focal length on the two nearest summits alone. Its sea horizon lies within about 5′ of the refracted globe's and about 45′ below the plane's, and Mont Agel stands 42′ above it, where the globe puts it within one pixel.
caus.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the photographed sea horizon at eye level, with Mont Agel below it.
mlo.title: Two places, one clock, two sunsets: Mauna Loa and the coast below it
mlo.mini: At 3,397 m on Mauna Loa, NOAA's sun-tracking instrument keeps the Sun after it has set at the coast 55 km away. On 104 clear evenings of 2016 its light stopped with the Sun's centre 1.7° below the horizontal (median).
mlo.text: Mauna Loa Observatory, 3,397 m up on Hawaii, records the direct sunlight every minute with a pyrheliometer that follows the Sun [1]. Keahole Point, on the coast 55 km towards the summer sunset, has no such instrument [2], so its sunset is computed. On a globe, the last ray that reaches the mountain grazes the sea some 220 km out, and the mountain keeps the Sun until its centre is 2.75° below the horizontal: 6 to 7 minutes after the coast. In 2016, on the 104 clear evenings when the observatory's horizon was the sea [3], the light stopped with the Sun's centre 1.72° below the horizontal (median), a median 1.9 minutes after the coast's computed sunset. It stops about a degree early because a ray grazing the sea is dimmed by hundreds of kilometres of low air. Refraction is standard: k = 0.13 near the ground [5] and 34′ beyond the tangent point [4]. In the cross-section the Earth is drawn smaller and the ground distances shortened, by the factors printed; the heights are true.
mlo.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the mountain's last direct light coming no later than the coast's on the same clear evening, measured by the same kind of instrument at both places. On a plane nothing is ever seen below eye level.
